title: Tic-Tac-Toe Deluxe
story: The grid. The pencil. The eternal battle of X versus O. You've played it a hundred times on scrap paper. Now YOU are the game engine. Build the board, take turns placing marks, check every row, column, and diagonal for three-in-a-row. Detect draws. Track who's winning across games. When your code declares 'X WINS!' after checking the top row, you'll feel like you just judged a championship match. This isn't just a game — it's the algorithm that decides victory.
why: Tic-tac-toe is the perfect synthesis of grid data structures (Vec of Vec), game state management with structs, win-condition algorithms, turn-based logic, and replay systems — a complete deterministic game engine.
analogy: A tennis umpire perched high above the court. They don't play — they observe, track every point, and declare the winner when the rules are met. Your code is the umpire: it watches the 3x3 grid, knows that three in a row (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal) ends the game, detects when all nine cells are full with no winner (draw), and keeps score across matches. The players bring the strategy; your code delivers the verdict.
try_it: Add an AI opponent! Simple strategy: 1) If AI can win, take the winning move. 2) If opponent can win, block it. 3) Take center if free. 4) Take a corner. 5) Take any remaining. Track wins/losses/draws across multiple games. Add a 'replay' feature that shows every move made.
tips: Win-checking has 8 lines: 3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals — check them systematically
A draw is when the board is full AND there's no winner — always check winner first
Use Cell enum for both players AND empty spaces — Empty means the cell is available
common_mistakes: Only checking the row/column/diagonal of the last move — a win could be anywhere on the board
Marking Cell.Empty as a winner — when all three cells are Empty they're technically equal, but that's not a win
Not using a 3x3 index bounds check before place_mark — row=5, col=5 would crash
